title: Rudin Ch 9: Functions of Several Variables

items.back: Standard linear algebra, with $\dim ℝ^{n}=n$.
$A(αx+βy)=αAx+βAy$. $L(X,Y)$ is the set of linear maps $X→Y$.
$f:E⊂ℝ^{n}→ℝ^{m}$ is differentiable at $x$ if some $A∈L(ℝ^{n},ℝ^{m})$ has $\dfrac{|f(x+h)−f(x)−Ah|}{|h|}→0$ as $h→0$. Write $f'(x)=A$.
$f'$ exists and $x↦f'(x)$ is continuous into $L(ℝ^{n},ℝ^{m})$.
$d(φ(x),φ(y))≤c\,d(x,y)$ for some $c<1$.
Rank = dimension of the range. $J_{f}(x)=\det f'(x)$.
A linear operator on a finite-dimensional space is one-to-one iff it is onto.
$\|A\|<∞$ and $A$ is uniformly continuous; $\|A+B\|≤\|A\|+\|B\|$; $\|BA\|≤\|B\|\|A\|$.

items.front: Invertible operators form an open set
items.back: If $A$ is invertible and $\|B−A\|\|A^{−1}\|<1$, then $B$ is invertible. Inversion is continuous.
The linear map $A$ in 9.11 is unique.
$(g∘f)'(x_{0})=g'(f(x_{0}))f'(x_{0})$ (composition of linear maps).
If $f$ is differentiable at $x$, all partials exist and $[f'(x)]$ is the matrix $(D_{j}f_{i}(x))$.
On a convex open set with $\|f'(x)\|≤M$: $|f(b)−f(a)|≤M|b−a|$.
$f∈\mathscr C'(E)$ iff all partials $D_{j}f_{i}$ exist and are continuous on $E$.
A contraction of a nonempty complete metric space has exactly one fixed point.
If $f$ is $\mathscr C'$ near $a$ and $f'(a)$ is invertible, there are open $U∋a$, $V∋f(a)$ with $f:U→V$ a bijection whose inverse is $\mathscr C'$.
If $f'(x)$ is invertible for every $x$, $f$ maps open sets to open sets.

If $f(a,b)=0$, $f∈\mathscr C'$ and $A_{x}$ (derivative in the $x$-variables) is invertible, then near $b$ there is a unique $\mathscr C'$ function $g$ with $g(b)=a$ and $f(g(y),y)=0$, and $g'(b)=−(A_{x})^{−1}A_{y}$.
A $\mathscr C'$ map of constant rank $r$ locally looks like a projection onto an $r$-dimensional subspace.
$\det(AB)=\det A\det B$; $A$ is invertible iff $\det A≠0$.
If $D_{1}f$, $D_{21}f$, $D_{2}f$ exist and $D_{21}f$ is continuous at a point, then $D_{12}f$ exists there and equals $D_{21}f$.
If $φ$ and $D_{2}φ$ are suitably continuous, $\dfrac{d}{dt}∫_{a}^{b}φ(x,t)dx=∫_{a}^{b}D_{2}φ(x,t)dx$.

items.modelProof: Start at any $x_{0}$ and iterate $x_{n+1}=φ(x_{n})$. Then $d(x_{n+1},x_{n})≤c^{n}d(x_{1},x_{0})$, so for $n<m$, $d(x_{n},x_{m})≤\dfrac{c^{n}}{1−c}d(x_{1},x_{0})$. The sequence is Cauchy; its limit $x$ satisfies $φ(x)=x$ by continuity. Two fixed points $x,y$ would give $d(x,y)≤c\,d(x,y)$, so $x=y$.

Write $f(x_{0}+h)=f(x_{0})+Ah+r(h)$ and $g(y_{0}+k)=g(y_{0})+Bk+s(k)$ with $r(h)/|h|→0$, $s(k)/|k|→0$. Substitute $k=Ah+r(h)$; the error $Br(h)+s(k)$ is $o(|h|)$ because $|k|≤(\|A\|+1)|h|$ for small $h$.

Let $A=f'(a)$, $λ$ with $2λ\|A^{−1}\|=1$, and a ball $U$ where $\|f'(x)−A\|<λ$. For each $y$, $φ(x)=x+A^{−1}(y−f(x))$ is a contraction on $U$ with $\|φ'\|≤1/2$, so $f$ is one-to-one on $U$. Show $V=f(U)$ is open, then prove the inverse is differentiable with derivative $f'(x)^{−1}$, which is continuous by 9.8.

items.prompt: Compute $f'(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=(x^{2}y,\ \sin(xy))$ and the derivative of $t↦f(t,t^{2})$ at $t=1$.
items.hint: Jacobian matrix, then the chain rule.

items.prompt: Show $f(x,y)=(x^{2}−y^{2},2xy)$ has invertible derivative at every point except the origin, but is not one-to-one on $ℝ^{2}∖\{0\}$.
Prove $\cos x=x$ has exactly one solution in $[0,1]$ using the contraction principle.
items.hint: Check that $\cos$ maps $[0,1]$ into itself and bound its derivative.
items.modelProof: $\cos([0,1])=[\cos1,1]⊂[0,1]$, and $|\cos x−\cos y|≤\sin(1)|x−y|$ with $\sin 1<1$. $[0,1]$ is complete, so 9.23 applies.

items.prompt: If all partial derivatives of $f$ exist at $p$, then $f$ is differentiable at $p$.
If $f$ is differentiable at $p$, then all partials exist at $p$.
If $f'(x)$ is invertible for every $x∈ℝ^{2}$, then $f$ is one-to-one.
If $d(φx,φy)<d(x,y)$ for all $x≠y$ in a complete space, then $φ$ has a fixed point.
Mixed partials $D_{12}f$ and $D_{21}f$ are always equal when both exist.
items.explanation: $xy(x^{2}−y^{2})/(x^{2}+y^{2})$ at the origin. Continuity is needed (9.41).
9.17 goes the other way: differentiable ⇒ partials exist. Here $f$ isn't even continuous at 0, so it can't be differentiable.

lines: Consecutive terms get close, so $(x_{n})$ is Cauchy and converges.
items.explanation: “Consecutive terms get close” does not make a sequence Cauchy ($\sqrt n$). The real argument sums the geometric bound: $d(x_{n},x_{m})≤Σ_{k=n}^{m−1}c^{k}d(x_{1},x_{0})≤c^{n}d(x_{1},x_{0})/(1−c)$.

items.name: $f(x,y)=\dfrac{xy}{x^{2}+y^{2}}$, $f(0,0)=0$
items.details: Both partials exist at the origin, but $f$ isn't even continuous there ($f=1/2$ along $y=x$).

items.name: $f(x,y)=\dfrac{xy(x^{2}−y^{2})}{x^{2}+y^{2}}$, $f(0,0)=0$
items.details: $\mathscr C'$ with both mixed partials existing at 0, but they are $+1$ and $−1$.

items.name: $(x,y)↦(e^{x}\cos y,\,e^{x}\sin y)$
items.details: Jacobian $e^{2x}≠0$ everywhere, so locally invertible everywhere, but not one-to-one (period $2π$ in $y$). The inverse function theorem is local.

items.name: $x+2x^{2}\sin(1/x)$
items.details: $f'(0)=1≠0$ but $f$ is not one-to-one near 0. The inverse function theorem needs $\mathscr C'$.

items.name: $φ(x)=\sqrt{1+x^{2}}$ on $ℝ$
items.details: $|φ(x)−φ(y)|<|x−y|$ for $x≠y$, but no fixed point. A contraction needs a fixed constant $c<1$.
